defaults.permitted_development: Across Greater London, a wraparound extension only stays within permitted development if the side and rear elements both satisfy Class A when read together. The combined footprint, leftover garden and mass at the rear corner are often what force the scheme into a full application.

rules.height_rules: Across Greater London, single-storey wraparounds still need to stay within the usual Class A height limits, with particular care on the side return where the 3m eaves rule can bite close to a boundary. The lower the side arm reads, the safer the design usually is.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to satisfy the normal rear-extension depth rules and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound cannot borrow generosity from one side of the design to excuse excess on the other.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Greater London, neighbour impact is usually judged at the side boundary and rear corner together. A scheme that looks acceptable in plan can still feel overbearing once those two faces are read as one mass.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof quiet and subordinate. The more the roof wraps around as one bulky form, the harder it is to argue that the work remains a modest householder addition.
rules.materials_rules: Materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the side-and-rear combination reads as one coherent addition rather than an oversized add-on.

rules.permitted_development: The wraparound fallback is narrow: both the side return and the rear projection have to satisfy Class A as one combined proposal. In Barking and Dagenham, the wraparound has to stay balanced; once the side return and rear wing start to eat up the plot together, the design stops looking modest.

rules.height_rules: Height is usually won or lost on the side return, where the standard Class A limits apply and the eaves can quickly become the critical number. In Barking and Dagenham, a visibly lower side-return roof is usually what keeps the whole composition from feeling like one continuous bulky block.
rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: A wraparound changes two boundaries at once, so the side return and the rear corner usually need to be read together rather than as separate walls. In Barking and Dagenham, the boundary question is whether the combined side-and-rear form crowds neighbouring space when the two elements are read as one.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. On tighter plots and in terraced or corner-plot streets, neighbour impact and street-scene fit are often the real deciding factors.

restrictions.conservation_area: In a conservation area, a wraparound has to stay visually quiet at the side return and rear corner so the original form of the house still reads clearly.
restrictions.listed_building: If the house is listed, a wraparound should be approached as heritage work, with listed building consent usually needed for any extension affecting character.
restrictions.article4_notes: The ordinary Class A route can still be displaced by an Article 4 direction, so the property-specific position should be checked before treating the wraparound as fallback development.

rules.depth_rules: The rear leg still has to meet the normal rear-extension depth rules, and the side leg must remain proportionate to the original house. A wraparound layout cannot borrow tolerance from one element to excuse the other.
rules.boundary_rules: With wraparounds, the harder boundary question is usually the combined effect of the side wall and the rear corner when seen from neighbouring gardens. In Westminster, tight boundaries mean the wraparound has to be judged as a sequence of impacts, not as one depth figure.
rules.roof_rules: Keep the roof simple and subordinate. Joined-up roofs that create a large boxy mass around the rear corner are more likely to need permission than a clearly secondary arrangement.
rules.materials_rules: External materials should match or sit comfortably with the existing house so the combined side-and-rear form does not look like an overgrown add-on. On tighter plots and in terraced or corner-plot streets, neighbour impact and street-scene fit are often the real deciding factors.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status usually tightens scrutiny on wraparounds because the side return and turning corner can alter character more than their footprint suggests.
restrictions.listed_building: If the house is listed, a wraparound should be approached as heritage work, with listed building consent usually needed for any extension affecting character.
restrictions.article4_notes: Local Article 4 controls can still cut back wraparound rights on specific sites, even where the wider area follows the normal national position.
